Part 4 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 3 · Throughput calculatorNext: 5 · Empirical rooflines

We now present a set of exercises to get a better grasp and intuition on those rooflines. Here, the idea is to perform some napkin math so the answers to those exercises is more about getting the formula and the leading order (or trend) right than it is about precise numerics.

Numbers and rules

Exercise 1: reading the roofline

Figure 15 · interactive

Roofline graph.

In Questions 1 and 2, we focus on the case of short context, i.e., a 1k context. Hence, the network can be approximated by its linear layers.

  1. Heights and throughput. What is the relationship between the heights of the two points and the throughput gain \(\Gamma\)?

    Solution

    First, let us describe what the roofline graph is plotting. On the roofline graph, the \(y\)-axis is describing how much FLOPs are consumed per second. We recall that one forward pass corresponds to \(F\) FLOPs. The time for one forward pass is the maximum between the time it takes to perform calculations and the time it takes to move bytes. Hence, we have

    \[ T = \max\left( \frac{F}{\pi}, \frac{Q}{\beta}\right), \]

    Hence, the attainable FLOP/s \(R\), i.e., the height of a point on the roofline graph, is given by

    \[ R = F/T = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{F \beta}{Q \pi}\right) = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{I}{I^\star}\right). \]

    Hence, on a logarithmic scale we have

    \[ \log_{10}(R) = \log_{10}(\pi) + \min\left( 0, \log_{10}(I) - \log_{10}(I^\star) \right). \]

    Denote \(\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\) and \(\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\). Then the ratio of the heights is given by

    \[ \frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}} = \frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}, I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)} . \]

    Now, we recall from Proposition 1 that, with \(\omega = Sr + 1\), \(S\) the number of denoising passes and \(r\) the cost of a denoising pass relative to a commit pass, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}},I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)}. \]

    Therefore, we get

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}}. \]

    This means that the throughput gain is proportional to the ratio of the heights on the roofline, with constant \(1/\omega\).

  2. The best batch. Find where on the graph \(\Gamma\) is largest, and estimate \(\Gamma\) there.

    Solution

    AR is memory-bound here, since its intensity is about 2, far below \(I^\star = 206\). Hence, according to Corollary 1, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \]

    Now, we have \(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} \leq \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) if and only if \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \leq I^\star\), since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \frac{b \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{\Pi}\). Hence, while TD is on the slope of the roofline graph, we have \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\).

    Since the network can be approximated by its linear layers, we have that \(\Pi \approx \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = \frac{\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)}{\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}\), where we recall that \(W^X\) is the number of weights, in parameters, that the method \(X\) reads. In particular, with a canvas size \(256\), we have that \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B) \approx W_{\mathrm{tot}}\), even at \(B=1\), since all the experts are touched. Since \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) increases with \(B\), \(\Pi\) is non-increasing in \(B\), and Corollary 1 (2) applies: \(\Gamma\) is largest at the batch \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\) at which TD reaches the ridge.

    Indeed, while TD is memory-bound, \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\) increases with \(B\). Once TD becomes compute-bound, i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \geq I^\star\), it stays compute-bound, since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1). Since \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) is also non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), \(\Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) then decreases. Hence, the optimal point is reached when TD just becomes compute-bound, i.e., just at the beginning of the flat roofline for TD.

    On the graph this happens for \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 6\), and the height ratio is then \(\approx 100\). Remembering the previous formula, we have then \(\Gamma \approx 100 / 15 \approx 6.5\), where we recall that \(\omega=15\).

  3. Large context. What changes at large context?

    Solution

    At large context, the KV cache carries most of the bytes and most of the FLOPs of both passes. Hence, according to Corollary 3, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{attn}}}}\right). \]

    A cache belongs to one sequence, so its bytes and FLOPs per sequence do not depend on the batch. Hence, at large context, the two points, and \(\Gamma\), no longer move with the batch.

    Now, on a global layer, a TD pass reads the same cache as an AR step and performs \(b\) times its FLOPs. Hence, we have that

    \[ \Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} = 1, \qquad \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8, \qquad \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 2{,}048. \]

    In particular, AR stays on the slope and TD on the roof, and the height ratio tends to \(I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}} \approx 206/8 \approx 26\). Therefore, we get

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega\, I_{\mathrm{attn}}} \approx \frac{26}{15} \approx 2. \]

Exercise 2: the gain along the batch

Figure 16

  1. Batch 1. Shrinking the canvas from 256 to 32 divides TPF by 8. Predict whether it also divides the penalty \(\Pi\) by 8, then give \(\Gamma\) at batch 1.

    Solution

    Let's have a look at the penalty. We are working at short context so the penalty is simply the ratio of the weights. We have that \(\Pi(1) = \frac{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(b)}{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(1)}\). Hence, ignoring the non-expert weights we have that

    \[ \Pi(1) \approx \frac{E}{k} \cdot \left[1 - \left(1-\frac{k}{E}\right)^b \right] . \]

    When \(b=32\), we have that

    \[\left(1-\frac{k}{E}\right)^b \approx 2^{-\frac{kb}{E \log(2)}} \approx 2^{-1.5 \cdot 2} \approx 1/8 .\]

    Hence, we have a reasonable approximation with \(\Pi(1) \approx \frac{E}{k} \approx 8\) no matter if \(b=256\) or if \(b=32\). The penalty is not divided by \(8\) in that scenario.

    Now, let us compute the throughput gain at \(B=1\). Since AR is memory bound, we have using Corollary 1, \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \] Since at \(B=1\) we also have that TD is memory bound, we have that \[\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} .\] Hence, we get that \(\Gamma \approx \frac{32}{16 \cdot 8} \approx 0.25 \). Contrary to the setting where \(b=256\), due to the linear penalty, in this case, AR has a throughput advantage at small batch size.

  2. TD starts winning. From which batch does TD win?

    Solution

    While TD is memory bound, we have that the throughput gain is given by \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\). We recall that \(\Pi(1) \approx 8\) hence, in order to find the batch at which TD wins we need to solve for \(B\) the following equation

    \[ \Pi(B) = \mathrm{TPF} \approx 2 .\]

    We recall that

    \[\Pi(B) \approx \frac{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{bB}}{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B}} .\]

    Since at \(B=1\) already have shown that \(\left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{bB}\approx 1/8\) we can approximate,

    \[\Pi(B) \approx \frac{1}{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B}} .\]

    Hence, we need to solve for

    \[ \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E} \right)^{B} \approx 1/2 . \]

    Now, we have the approximation

    \[\left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B} \approx 2^{\frac{kB}{E\log(2)}} \approx 2^{\frac{1.5 \cdot kB}{E}} .\]

    Hence, we get that

    \[ 1.5 \cdot k B \approx E . \]

    Hence, we have \(B \approx 16 / 1.5 \approx 11\). In reality, we have that \(B\) is slightly lower with \(B \approx 8\). The main reason for this approximation is because we have neglected the non-expert weights.

  3. The best batch. At which batch size is the gain maximal?

    Solution

    We know from ??? that the multiplicative throughput gain \(\Gamma\) is maximal when TD is just compute bound. In practice, we have that, recalling that we operate in bf16 precision and that at batch size 1, we already have that the canvas touches all the experts,

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{TD}} \approx \frac{2 N_{act}bB}{2 W_{tot}} =\approx bB \frac{W_{ne} + L k W^e}{W_{ne} + L E W^e} \]

    This can be simplified in

    \[\class{mj-td}{I^{TD}} \approx \frac{bBk}{E} \frac{1 + \frac{W_{ne}}{L k W^e}}{1 + \frac{W_{ne}}{L E W^e}} .\]

    Now, a lower bound on \(\class{mj-td}{I^{TD}}\) would be given by \(\frac{bBk}{E}\) but this is conservative. Instead, we have using that \(W_{ne} / W^e \approx 300\) and \(L=30\) that

    \[ \frac{W_{ne}}{L k W^e} \approx \frac{10}{8} \approx 1 ,\]

    and

    \[ \frac{W_{ne}}{L E W^e} \approx \frac{1}{16}\]

    Hence, we have

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{TD}} \approx \frac{2kbB}{E} . \]

    We solve for \(\class{mj-td}{I^{TD}} = I^\star \) and we have that

    \[ B \approx \frac{200 \cdot 128}{2 \cdot 8 \cdot 32} \approx 50 . \]

    On the graph, we have that TD becomes compute bound around \(B \approx 41\), hence our result is a reasonable approximation.

  4. TD loses again. At which batch does AR catch up? Predict whether this batch depends on \(b\).

    Solution

    Beyond \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\), TD is compute-bound. Hence, according to Corollary 1, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}. \]

    Therefore, \(\Gamma = 1\) when

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} = \frac{I^\star}{\omega} \approx \frac{206}{15} \approx 14. \]

    In particular, \(b\) does not appear.

    Now, from the previous question we have

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}} \approx \frac{kB}{E} \frac{1 + \frac{W_{ne}}{LkW^e}}{1 + \frac{W_{ne}}{EkW^e}} \approx 2 \frac{kB}{E} .\]

    Hence, solving for \(B\), we obtain that

    \[ B \approx \frac{14 \cdot 128}{2 \cdot 8} \approx 100 .\]

    On the graph, we have that AR wins again in terms of throughput when \(B \approx 100\) as well. Hence our approximation is reasonable.

Exercise 3: a dense model

We take a dense model, Llama 3.1 8B, on the H200, with \(b = 256\) and \(S = 14\), and pair it with a TD twin that has no self-conditioning. A dense model has no expert penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = 1\), and in BF16 its linear intensity is the batch: \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) = 2BN_{\mathrm{act}}/(2N_{\mathrm{act}}) = B\).

Figure 17

Roofline for a dense model

  1. No penalty. With \(\Pi = 1\), one can expect \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF} \approx 17\) at batch 1 and short context. Find the flaw, give \(\Gamma\), and give the parity batch.

    Solution

    First, at batch 1 and short context, AR's intensity is \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 1\), far below \(I^\star = 206\), so AR is memory bound. Hence, we recall that according to Corollary 1 (1) we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min \left( \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) = \min \left( \mathrm{TPF}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \]

    Hence, \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}\) if and only if \(\mathrm{TPF} \leq \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\), i.e., if and only if TD is memory bound. The main flaw in the reasoning is to assume that TD is memory bound. While it was true in Exercise 2, it is no longer true for a dense model which is more favorable to TD. Indeed, since there is no penalty, and since we are considering the bf16 precision model, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \frac{2 b B N_{\mathrm{act}}}{2 W_{\mathrm{tot}}} = bB, \]

    since \(N_{\mathrm{act}} = W_{\mathrm{tot}}\) for a dense model. Hence, at batch size \(B=1\) we already have \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 256 \geq I^\star = 206\). Therefore, TD is compute bound and, with \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}(1) = 1\), we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}(1)} = \frac{206}{15 \cdot 1} \approx 14 . \]

    This is slightly lower than \(\mathrm{TPF} \approx 17\). Indeed, per committed token, TD reads 256 times fewer bytes than AR, but only up to the ridge, 206, of this can be turned into speed, hence the factor \(206/256 \approx 0.8\).

    Next, since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 256B\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), TD stays compute bound at every batch. Hence, recalling that \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} = B\), we have \(\Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega B}\), which decreases with the batch, so that the best batch is batch 1 (Corollary 1 (2a)). To find the parity batch, we solve for

    \[ B = \frac{I^\star}{\omega} = \frac{206}{15} \approx 14 . \]

    On the map, which also counts the 1k cache, \(\Gamma \approx 13\) at batch 1 and parity is at batch 15. Indeed, the cache, at intensity 4, raises AR's intensity at batch 1 and lowers it near batch 14.

  2. Large batch. At a 1k context, can any batch make AR compute-bound?

    Solution

    First, we recall that for AR, we have that \(\class{mj-ar}{F^{AR}} = 2 B N_{act}\), since a step performs 2 FLOPs per active parameter and per token. Regarding the bytes that need to be transferred, we have that for large batch \(\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}} \approx 2 \cdot 2 \cdot B C L h n_{kv} \). The first 2 comes from the fact that we are storing both the keys and the values and the second 2 comes from the bf16 precision. We have that

    \[ C L h n_{kv} \approx 1000 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 \cdot 8 \approx 3.3 \times 10^{7} ,\]

    so that a sequence reads \(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3.3 \times 10^{7} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{8}\) bytes of cache, i.e., 0.13 GB. On the other hand, we have \(7 \times 10^9 \) parameters, which are shared by the batch: they add \(2 \cdot 7 \times 10^{9}/B\) bytes per sequence, which vanish as \(B \to \infty\), while the cache belongs to one sequence and stays. Hence, \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}}\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), and its limit as \(B \to \infty\) bounds it at every batch. Hence, we get that, for very large batches

    \[\class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}} \to \frac{2 \cdot 7 \times 10^{9}}{1.3 \times 10^{8}} \approx 107 \lt I^\star .\]

    Therefore, no batch makes AR compute bound at a 1k context.

Exercise 4: the vocabulary matrix

We go back to DiffusionGemma on the H200, with \(b = 256\) and a 1k context. As in Exercise 1, the network can be approximated by its linear layers. Proposition 1 ignores the vocabulary matrix (Part 1, What the formulas leave out). AR applies it once per step, as its head. TD applies it in every pass, as its head and, for self-conditioning, as a soft embedding of the prediction of the previous pass. In this exercise, we count both uses in all \(\omega = 15\) passes, commit included, which is what the engine runs; the maps of this chapter leave out the two uses whose output is discarded. The logits and probabilities that these uses write to HBM and read back are counted in FP32, \(\class{mj-ar}{\lambda^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 2\) and \(\class{mj-td}{\lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 5\) times per output position (Figure 18).

Figure 18 · interactive

The logits of one position cross HBM twice in an AR step and five times in a denoising pass of DiffusionGemma.

Each arrow is one move of a vector of \(V\) numbers between a kernel and HBM, counted at 4 bytes per number as in the exact accounting of Part 3; \(\lambda\) is the number of arrows per output position. Self-conditioning adds the three moves of the next pass: its softmax reads the logits \(\ell\) and writes the probabilities \(p\), and its soft embedding reads \(p\). The softmax and the soft embedding run in 13 of the 14 denoising passes, so a canvas makes 67 moves per position; the cost model charges \(\class{mj-td}{\lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 5\) to all 14 passes, i.e., 70.

  1. The lookup. A token also enters the network through the matrix, as its input embedding. Why can we ignore this use?

    Solution

    The input embedding is a lookup: it copies the row of the matrix indexed by the token. Hence, it performs no FLOPs and reads \(d\) parameters per position, i.e., \(2d \approx 5.6\) kB in BF16. On the other hand, the head and the soft embedding multiply by the whole matrix, which costs \(2Vd \approx 1.5\) GFLOPs per position and reads \(2Vd \approx 1.5\) GB per use. Hence, the embeddings of the 256 positions of a TD pass take about 1.4 MB per sequence, i.e., 0.1% of one read of the matrix, and we ignore the lookup.

  2. The accounting. How many FLOPs and bytes does the matrix add to a TD pass and to an AR step at batch \(B\)?

    Solution

    First, the head multiplies the activations of a position, a vector of size \(d\), by the matrix, which gives \(V\) logits for \(2Vd\) FLOPs. The soft embedding multiplies a distribution over the \(V\) tokens by the matrix, which gives a vector of size \(d\) for the same \(2Vd\) FLOPs. A TD pass applies both to its \(bB\) positions, and an AR step applies the head to its \(B\) positions. Hence, we have that

    \[ \Delta \class{mj-td}{F^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 2 \cdot 2BbdV, \]

    and

    \[ \Delta \class{mj-ar}{F^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 2BdV. \]

    In particular, since the rest of the network costs \(2N_{\mathrm{act}} \approx 6.2\) GFLOPs per position, the matrix raises the FLOPs of a TD pass by \(3.0/6.2 \approx 48\%\) and those of an AR step by \(1.5/6.2 \approx 24\%\).

    Regarding the bytes, the matrix holds \(Vd \approx 0.74\)B parameters, i.e., \(2Vd \approx 1.5\) GB in BF16, read once per use and shared by the batch. In a TD pass, the soft embedding and the head are two products at the two ends of the pass, and the matrix is far larger than the L2 cache of the GPU, so a TD pass reads it twice. Moreover, each output position writes and reads a vector of \(V\) numbers \(\lambda\) times, at 4 bytes per number, i.e., \(4\lambda V\) bytes. Hence, with \(\class{mj-td}{\lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 5\) and \(\class{mj-ar}{\lambda^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 2\), we have that

    \[ \Delta \class{mj-td}{Q^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 2 \cdot 2dV + 20BbV, \]

    and

    \[ \Delta \class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 2dV + 8BV. \]

    Numerically, \(\Delta \class{mj-td}{Q^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 2.95 + 1.34\,B\) GB and \(\Delta \class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 1.5\) GB, since the logits of an AR step take 2.1 MB per sequence. In particular, unlike the matrix, the logits of TD grow with the batch.

  3. The intensities. How does the matrix move the intensities of AR and TD? Does TD reach the ridge earlier or later?

    Solution

    First, let \(F\) and \(Q\) be the FLOPs and bytes of a pass without the matrix, and \(I = F/Q\) its intensity. Then we have that

    \[ I' = \frac{F + \Delta F}{Q + \Delta Q} = (1 - \theta)\, I + \theta\, I_V, \]

    with

    \[ I_V = \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta Q}, \qquad \theta = \frac{\Delta Q}{Q + \Delta Q}. \]

    Hence, the intensity with the matrix is a weighted average of the intensity without it and of the intensity \(I_V\) of the matrix, and the matrix raises the intensity if and only if \(I_V \gt I\).

    For AR, using Question 2, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_V} = \frac{2BdV}{2dV + 8BV} = \frac{Bd}{d + 4B} \approx B, \]

    since \(B \ll d/4 \approx 700\). On the other hand, \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) = BN_{\mathrm{act}}/\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B) \le B\), since \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B) \ge \class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(1) = N_{\mathrm{act}}\). Hence, the matrix raises the intensity of AR at every batch. Indeed, it behaves as a dense layer, whose weights are all shared by the batch, whereas additional sequences make AR read new experts. For instance, at batch 6, the intensity of AR grows from 2.1 to 2.4, far below the ridge.

    For TD, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}_V} = \frac{4BbdV}{4dV + 20BbV} = \frac{Bbd}{d + 5Bb}, \]

    which tends to \(d/5 \approx 563\) as \(B\) grows. Without the logits, we would have \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}_V} = bB\). With them, each position adds \(4dV\) FLOPs and \(20V\) bytes, which caps \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}_V}\) at \(d/5\). On the other hand, \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}_{\mathrm{lin}}} = bBN_{\mathrm{act}}/W_{\mathrm{tot}} \approx 32B\) grows without bound, and the two are equal at \(B \approx 15\). Hence, the matrix raises the intensity of TD below batch 15 and lowers it above. In particular, at batch 6 the intensity of TD grows from 194 to 234, past the ridge. Solving for the ridge with the matrix, we get that

    \[ \frac{256\,B \cdot (6.2 + 3.0)}{49 + 2.95 + 1.34\,B} = 206, \]

    with the FLOPs in GFLOPs and the bytes in GB, i.e., \(B \approx 5.1\), against \(B \approx 6.4\) without the matrix. Therefore, TD reaches the ridge earlier.

  4. The gain at large batch. Above the best batch, by what factor does the matrix change \(\Gamma\)? Does Proposition 1 overstate or understate the gain there?

    Solution

    The throughput of a decoder is inversely proportional to the time of its pass. Hence, denoting by \(s = T'/T\) the slowdown of a decoder due to the matrix, we have that

    \[ \frac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma} = \frac{\class{mj-ar}{s^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{\class{mj-td}{s^{\mathrm{TD}}}}. \]

    Now, from batch 6.4 on, TD is compute-bound with and without the matrix (Question 3). Hence, its time is \(F/\pi\), and we have that

    \[ \class{mj-td}{s^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 1 + \frac{\Delta \class{mj-td}{F^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-td}{F^{\mathrm{TD}}}} = 1 + \frac{4Vd}{2N_{\mathrm{act}}}, \]

    i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{s^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 1 + 3.0/6.2 \approx 1.48\).

    On the other hand, AR is memory-bound with and without the matrix (Question 3). Hence, its time is \(Q/\beta\), and we have that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{s^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 1 + \frac{\Delta \class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}}} \approx 1 + \frac{0.74}{\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}, \]

    with \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) in billions. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \frac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma} \approx \frac{1 + 0.74/\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}{1.48}. \]

    At batch 8, AR reads about 11B parameters, so the factor is \(1.07/1.48 \approx 0.72\). Once AR reads all 24.5B parameters, it is \(1.03/1.48 \approx 0.70\). Hence, above the best batch, Proposition 1 overstates \(\Gamma\) by about 1.4, almost independently of the batch. Indeed, TD pays for the matrix in FLOPs at all its positions, whereas AR pays for it in bytes shared by the batch. The cost model, which counts 27 uses per TD position and the cache, gives 1.36 at batch 110.

Exercise 5: sparse attention

We go back to the H200 and replace DiffusionGemma's five global layers with the sparse layers of Remark 1 (Table 3), as in Figure 11.

  1. The limit. As the context grows, does TD win with \(S = 14\)? Up to which \(S\) does it win? Predict, then check the case \(S = 14\) against the shading of Figure 11, which is drawn for \(S = 14\).

    Solution

    As the context grows, the index scan carries most of the bytes and most of the FLOPs of both passes. Hence, according to Corollary 3 (2), we have that \(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} \to 1\), and

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 16, \]

    and

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 4{,}096. \]

    Since \(16 \lt 206 \lt 4{,}096\), TD's scan is compute-bound and AR's is memory-bound. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega I_{\mathrm{idx}}} \approx \frac{206}{15 \cdot 16} \approx 0.86. \]

    Hence, AR wins. Indeed, AR runs its scan at \(16/206 \approx 8\%\) of the peak, and per committed token TD's 15 passes at the peak take longer than AR's step, since \(15 \gt 206/16 \approx 13\).

    Now, only \(\omega = Sr + 1\) depends on \(S\). Hence, \(\Gamma \propto 1/\omega\) at every batch and context, and TD wins in the limit when

    \[ \frac{206}{16\,\omega} \gt 1, \]

    i.e., when \(\omega \lt 13\), i.e., \(S \le 11\).

    Dense attention, at \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\), allows \(S \le 24\). Note that the limit assumes \(b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} \gt I^\star\), i.e., a canvas of at least 13 positions. On a shorter canvas, both scans are memory-bound, and \(\Gamma \to \mathrm{TPF}\), which is below 1. In Figure 11, the shaded region \(\Gamma \lt 1\) reaches the right edge.

  2. Far from the limit. At 4M tokens, Figure 11 is shaded: Corollary 3 gives \(\Gamma \lt 1\). Does AR win at batch 1 with \(S = 14\)? Find the assumption that fails.

    Solution

    Corollary 3 assumes that attention carries most of the bytes. The index cache holds 640 B per token, so 4M tokens take 2.7 GB. On the other hand, at batch 1, AR reads 6.2 GB of weights and 0.2 GB of window cache. Hence, the assumption fails: the weights still carry about 0.7 of AR's bytes, and the index cache about 0.3. Therefore, according to Proposition 2, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 0.7 \cdot 1 + 0.3 \cdot 16 \approx 5.5. \]

    Now, TD's 256 queries select \(U_{C,m}(b) = C\,[1 - (1 - m/C)^b] \approx 490\)k distinct tokens, slightly fewer than \(bm \approx 520\)k since \(bm = C/8\), i.e., about 10 GB of global cache. Hence, TD reads about \(49 + 2.7 + 10 \approx 62\) GB against AR's 9.1 GB, and

    \[ \Pi \approx 6.8, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} \approx \frac{17}{6.8} \approx 2.5, \]

    while

    \[ \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}} \approx \frac{206}{15 \cdot 5.5} \approx 2.5. \]

    Hence, according to Corollary 1, TD sits at the ridge, \(\Gamma \approx 2.5\), and TD wins.

    Parity at batch 1 needs \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 14\), hence an index cache near 87% of AR's bytes, i.e., about 42 GB or 65M tokens. At 4M tokens, the global cache alone is about 85 GB, and the 141 GB of an H200 hold the weights and at most about 4.3M tokens of cache. Therefore, on one H200, the limit of Question 1 is out of reach.

Exercise 6: number formats

We keep DiffusionGemma on the H200 at a 1k context, and change the format of the weights, of the KV cache and of the matrix multiplications. A format of \(s\) bytes per value multiplies the intensity of what it stores by \(2/s\): \(s_w\) acts on \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{kv}}\) on \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 4g/(\kappa^c_\ell s_{\mathrm{kv}})\) (Definitions 1–3). The format of a multiplication sets the peak, and hence the ridge, at which its FLOPs run. The questions follow the roofline chapter of How to Scale Your Model, which compares int8 weights with BF16 and with int8 multiplications.

  1. A common speed-up. Weights and cache are in FP8, and every multiplication, attention included, runs at the FP8 peak. A colleague argues that this favours TD, which is compute-bound at its best batch and gains from the doubled peak. Find the flaw: does \(\Gamma\) change?

    Solution

    We recall from Proposition 1 that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}},I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)}. \]

    In FP8, every value takes 1 byte instead of 2, so every intensity doubles. Since every multiplication runs at the FP8 peak, the ridge \(I^\star\) doubles as well. Hence, both minima double, and \(\Gamma\) does not change, at any batch or context. In particular, a memory-bound AR step reads half the bytes, so it also runs twice as fast.

    A format changes \(\Gamma\) only when it speeds up the bytes and the FLOPs by different factors. For instance, take an FP8 cache read by BF16 attention. Then \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) doubles to 16, while the ridge of attention stays at 206. Hence, according to Corollary 3, the long-context limit becomes

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{206}{15 \cdot 16} \approx 0.86, \]

    as with the index scan of Exercise 5.

  2. Fewer bytes than FLOPs. NVFP4 weights, once on the H200, which has no FP4 multiplication and converts them to BF16, and once on the B200, which multiplies them at its FP4 peak; the cache stays in BF16. Predict which setting acts like a lower BF16 ridge, then give each one's best gain.

    Solution

    Weights of \(s_w\) bytes multiply the linear intensities by \(2/s_w\), and multiplications that run \(\sigma\) times faster than BF16 multiply the ridge by \(\sigma\). We recall from Question 1 that \(\Gamma\) depends only on the intensities divided by the ridge. Hence, each setting acts like BF16 on an accelerator with ridge \(\rho I^\star\), where

    \[ \rho = \frac{\sigma}{2/s_w}. \]

    With \(s_w \approx 0.56\) (Table 3), we have \(2/s_w \approx 3.6\). We neglect the BF16 cache, which at 1k tokens is a sixth to a quarter of AR's bytes at these batches once the weights are in NVFP4, and which raises the best gains below by about 10% on the H200 and 1% on the B200. At \(b = 256\), we recall from Question 3 of Exercise 2 that, with all experts touched, \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 256 \cdot 3.1\, B/24.5 \approx 32B\).

    On the H200, \(\sigma = 1\). Hence, \(\rho = 1/3.6\), and the ridge is \(206/3.6 \approx 57\). Hence, the corner is at \(32B \approx 57\), i.e., \(B \approx 1.8\). There, AR touches \(128\,[1 - (15/16)^{1.8}] \approx 14\) experts per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 14 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 4.2\)B parameters. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{1.8 \cdot 3.1}{4.2} \approx 1.3, \]

    and

    \[ \Gamma \approx \frac{57}{15 \cdot 1.3} \approx 2.9. \]

    On the B200, \(\sigma = 4\). Hence, \(\rho = 4/3.6 \approx 1.1\), and the ridge is \(1{,}125/3.6 \approx 310\). Hence, the corner is at \(32B \approx 310\), i.e., near batch 10. There, AR leaves \(2^{-0.94} \approx 0.52\) of the experts untouched, touches 61 per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 61 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 12.7\)B parameters. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{10 \cdot 3.1}{12.7} \approx 2.4, \]

    and

    \[ \Gamma \approx \frac{310}{15 \cdot 2.4} \approx 8.6, \]

    against about 8 at the B200's BF16 ridge of 281.

    Hence, when the weight bytes shrink by more than the multiplications speed up, \(\rho \lt 1\), and the setting acts like a lower ridge, which lowers both the best batch and the best gain (Corollary 2). This is the case of NVFP4 on the H200, and of FP8 weights converted to BF16 on an A100, which has no FP8 rate: \(\rho = 1/2\), so the batch at which a multiplication becomes compute-bound halves, as in How to Scale Your Model. On the other hand, NVFP4 on the B200 has \(\rho \gt 1\) and acts like a higher ridge. Finally, at batch 1, every setting keeps both decoders on the slope, and \(\Gamma \approx 2.2\).
